main.label: good
main.text: Node holds a value and a next pointer. In pushFront, new Node{value, head} allocates a node whose next is the current head, and then head is set to the new node. So the new node becomes the first node of the list and links to what used to be first.

followUp.label: good
followUp.text: The order is what matters: the new node takes the old head as its next before head is moved, so the rest of the list is not lost. On an empty list head is nullptr, so the new node's next is nullptr and it is both the first and the last node.

main.label: good
main.text: The destructor walks the list from head. It saves the current node in temp, moves head to head->next, and then deletes temp. Every node was allocated with new in pushFront, so every one has to be deleted, and keeping temp first means I never lose the pointer to the rest of the list. It runs automatically when list goes out of scope at the end of main.

followUp.label: good
followUp.text: With three nodes it deletes them one at a time, 1 then 2 then 3, and head ends up nullptr. Without the destructor the memory from the three new calls would be leaked.

main.label: good
main.text: removeFront first checks head == nullptr. On an empty list it returns false immediately and does not touch out or delete anything, so the only effect is the false return value telling the caller that nothing was removed.

followUp.label: good
followUp.text: The caller checks the bool before using the removed value, and out is left unchanged. Without that check, head->next would dereference a null pointer and the program would crash.

main.label: good
main.text: pushFront(3), then (2), then (1), each new node goes in front, so the list is 1 2 3. The first print() outputs '1 2 3'. removeFront takes the front value 1, so main prints 'Removed 1', and the second print() outputs '2 3'. The list reads in reverse of the insertion order because each push goes to the front.

followUp.label: good
followUp.text: The values were inserted as 3, 2, 1 but read as 1 2 3, which is reverse insertion order, because the most recent push is always the head.

main.label: good
main.text: If pushFront added at the end, the list would read 3 2 1, the same as the insertion order. The first print() would output '3 2 1', removeFront would remove 3 so main prints 'Removed 3', and the last print() would output '2 1'. Where the new node is inserted decides the order of the list.

followUp.label: good
followUp.text: Appending would also need a walk to the last node or a tail pointer, but the visible change is that the printed order matches the insertion order instead of being reversed.
